utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there are no preliminaries, I would ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Vanderpuye will now continue his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Yesterday when we left off, I indicated I was going to a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So if I could have, please, P1361 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for your reference, Colonel this is the 17 July intercept that you were shown by Mr. Stojanovic yesterday. It is timed at 11.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please talk in the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not going to go the whole of the intercept with you. We have your evidence concerning your views or recollection concerning your purported participation in this intercept, as we can see at the bottom of the page in the English. And I think we'll have to go to the second page in the B/C/S. But, for the time being, what I wanted to ask you about are just a couple of things. The first thing is you say you have no recollection of speaking to Kovac who you identified, I think, as the deputy minister or the minister of the interior at the time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the second page in the B/C/S, you'll see the reference to this part of the conversation concerning Kovac. And it says in the intercept: "I know," that's X speaking. "Salapura talked to Kovac and got his verbal consent that the shift will arrive in the course of the day." Now, you may not know this, but it's the Prosecution's position that this intercept concerns the engagement of VRS and MUP forces to sweep the area of Cerska, among other areas, beginning on the 17th of July, 1995. But what I want to ask you is that in order for the commander of the Main Staff to issue an order for MUP units to be engaged in such conduct, would that require the consent or the approval of the Ministry of the Interior, that is, either the minister or the deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I suppose so. It would have been a joint action of the forces of the military police, police, and so on. And other available forces that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go to the first page in the B/C/S, and we'll stay, I think, on this page in the English. Yes, I can -- I think we -- you can see the other reference to your name, it's near the bottom, about three lines or four lines from the bottom. In that part of the conversation, X says: "I told the commander he ordered Salapura and the order will be drafted, or rather, a request to the MUP to bring back all of them, in fact to keep them." So what I wanted to know from you is: With respect to the consent or the authorisation that's required in order for the commander of the Main Staff to engage MUP units, is that something that has to be in writing or can it be done in another form?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is completely illogical. No communication between the commander of the Main Staff and MUP went through me. It went through the security service. I didn't have any such units that I would have any power over which would be involved in the sweep operations. They could have been units of the military police or some other available units. I don't understand this document at all and I can state under full responsibility that I have nothing to do with this, and that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, you're not here to defend yourself; you're here to answer questions. The question was whether such orders would be given in writing, yes or no. That was the simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't say now what the practice was. I was not privy to such orders. It depended on where they were. If they were together, they could have made such arrangements verbally; if they were not in the same place, then this would have had to be done in writing, both by the asking party, the requesting party, and the requested party. I can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have answered the question. That is, that you do not know the practice. Therefore, listen carefully to the questions that are put to the you and try to answer those. Mr. Vanderpuye, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You may recall, Colonel, you were asked about the accuracy of intercepted communications I think rather generally by my colleague Mr. Stojanovic and you said at some point, yes, mistakes can be made, and this related to this particular intercept as concerns whether the conversation occurred with Kovacevic or Kovac. You remember that part of your evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I want to show you is P1582. But before we go there, I just want to go back to the second page in the B/C/S for a second. Okay. And near -- near the end of this conversation you'll see the part that I just read to you before regarding your purported conversation with Kovac. And then it says that you: "... got his verbal consent that the shift will arrive in the course of the day." I just want you to keep that in mind because I'm going to show you the next document, which is 1582, P1582.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you have now in front of you is an order that's issued by Goran Saric who was the commander of the special police brigade of the MUP. In the header you'll see that this is dated 17 July 1995. It's directed to the Ministry of the Interior. It is also directed to - and I want you to keep this in mind as well - to the Zvornik CJB, public security centre, and it's an order as can you see there. What this calls for is for the establishment in paragraph 1 of combat group, a combat group, of police and it lists what units in particular. Doboj Special Police Detachment, two companies from Jahorina, two PJP special police units, and so on and so forth. And it says: "In the course of today, to search the terrain of Pobudje sector in the course of today," which we saw previously in the intercept, "17 July 1995 and fully mop-up the right side of Milici, Drinjaca road before regrouping for the search of Cerska." To your knowledge of how a unit may be subordinated or resubordinated to the VRS, a MUP unit, that is, is this document consistent with what we saw in the intercept that I showed you a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see here is that the police unit from this conversation is being engaged in the sweep-up of the terrain in the Drinjaca area. I can state for a fact that I was not familiarised with this, that I had nothing to do with it. I can state that neither I nor any of my organs were ever engaged in search operations of the terrain. This is the sort of job that the State Security Service [as interpreted] would be involved and the military police, but not the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I mean to ask, if I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to say to Mr. Salapura that that was -- he's not answering the question. Can he please answer the question. He was warned not to defend himself but to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe I can rephrase it a little bit better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, just one intervention although it's not my witness. It says here "State Security Service." I don't think that it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, are you able to clarify whether or not you referred to the State Security Service in your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The second question, and that related to the one that I previously asked you, about whether or not this was consistent with what we saw in the intercept. Let me try and rephrase it a little bit. Is the fact that that Goran Saric issued an order to special police brigade units to be engaged in the search of the terrain around Cerska consistent with the resubordination of that unit to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would not be consistent with the resubordination of a unit, because in that case, it should read here that the unit which is within the jurisdiction of Goran Saric, in other words the special unit, should be subordinated to the Vlasenica Brigade, say, in order to mop-up such and such a terrain in the area of Cerska and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you another document. I'm sorry, you're not finished your answer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't. This means that the police unit is independently carrying out this assignment in keeping with a decision that was issued earlier on between MUP and the Drina Corps but I don't know at which level.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you another document. And before we go to that document, I want you to keep in mind what units we're talking about in this document, which is specifically referring to the units that are engaged in the mopping-up of the right side of the Milici-Drinjaca road. So let's go to the next one, which is P1579. What you should have in front of you - and I think you do - is an order that's issued by your commander, General Mladic, 17 July 1995 and can you see that it refers to the integration of operations to crush lagging Muslim forces. And it's an order. That is -- can you see that it says "order," "naradjenje"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of this order, we see that General Mladic assigns Nedjo Trkulja, Milovan Stankovic, and Bogdan Sladojevic to assist in joining the VRS and MUP forces the planning and co-ordination of combat operations to block, crush, destroy lagging Muslim forces in the wider areas of Kamenica and Cerska. Do you see that in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. So it's a group which is supposed to co-ordinate the joint activities of the MUP and the army. It does not follow from this that the MUP unit was resubordinated to any of the units of the VRS. And now there's a co-ordinating group, which will be there for both sides so as to avoid overlap, losses as a result of that, to avoid having swaths of terrain that are not covered by either side. So it's a co-ordinating body which is monitoring the developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me take you down to paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Vanderpuye, could I keep the witness for a moment with paragraph 1. You are emphasizing the co-ordination efforts. If I read this document well, it says: "To assist in the joining of the VRS and MUP forces, the planning and co-ordination of combat operations ..." Now, you have not commented on the words "the joining of the VRS and MUP forces," that is, that they are joined and then, of course, operate in co-ordination. Is there any comment you would have on the words "joining of the VRS and the MUP forces ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. Joining up or combining in our military terminology means co-ordination and activity that would be focussed on the same goal. So you would be co-ordinating the activities of both these sets of units in order to achieve the set goal. This is what I was discussing earlier on. But for that purpose, the MUP unit has not been resubordinated to the VRS unit in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the reference to the co-ordination later is superfluous because it is already comprised in the joining, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But throughout the operation, somebody has to co-ordinate it and follow where each of the units is located, whether one is ahead of the other and so on. Because that group does not have a commander of its own. It doesn't have somebody who is in charge because no one unit is resubordinated to the other, neither the VRS unit to the MUP unit, nor the MUP unit to the VRS unit. That -- hence, the co-ordinating body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you a different question, but the beginning of your answer related to my question, at least to some extent. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, I was going to paragraph number 3 in this document. And bearing in mind that this is an order, I want you to take a look at it. In particular, what it says is that: "As of 17 July, the forces of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, the 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade, the 67th Communication Regiment, the military police of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, and MUP forces engaged in the wider areas of Bratunac" and again we see this particular unit, those that are particularly engaged in Milici and Drinjaca, "will comb the terrain in the zone of the Bratunac, Drinjaca, Milici, Beslici village with the aim of discovering and destroying lagging Muslim groups." Is that not an order with respect to the activities of not only VRS units but the MUP units indicated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order from the commander of the Main Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you one other document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask another question. In that paragraph 3, it is also said that the author appoints Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic as the commander of all the aforementioned forces during the conduct of the aforementioned task. Now, whatever may have happened, is that an expression of subordinating all of the forces to the command of this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is a different matter. In this case, yes, an individual is being placed in charge of commanding both the VRS units engaged in that particular assignment and the MUP. And that individual is Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic or Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least he is being appointed as such. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just -- Mr. Salapura, you just mentioned the date of 19th of July. What do you mean by that? The document dates of 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And refers to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I saw down there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and refers to the 19th of July as the date by which the completion of the task should have been.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your comment was not in response to a question and was not accurate in reflection of what the document says. You may proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to show the Colonel the document that he was shown yesterday, it's a 13 July document. Bear with me, I'll give you the P number -- sorry it's a D number, D00306. You'll remember, Mr. President, this is the one with the -- for which we submitted a translation request. And I think we have a translation but it's not yet uploaded to e-court, and I want to see if we can show it in a different way. Okay. I think we can show the updated English translation. I think we can show the updated English translation in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's all right. We can work with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I want to deal with with this particular document is not so much the substance. But you testified yesterday at transcript page 13042 that General Tolimir would have received this document. You may remember that Mr. Stojanovic asked you about that. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just briefly read back what you --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yes. This is addressed to the sector, and General Tolimir should have received this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now I just want to establish a couple of things. One is that: On the night of 13 July, who in the Main Staff, in the sector of security and intelligence, was present besides yourself and your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tolimir had his secretary in the sector only, Spasoje Zelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the security administration, just as in my case, it was a different administration. And in the sector itself, Tolimir was the chief of sector, and he only had his secretary there. And you asked me about the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, who under the sector, that is, either in the intelligence administration or in the security administration, besides yourself and your subordinates, was present on the night of 13 July 1995 at the command of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was there anybody within the sector, either in the security side or the intelligence side, higher ranking than you present there that night, that is, night of 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Main Staff there was General Miletic present, as far as I remember; he was the chief of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm talking about within the sector of intelligence and security. You indicated that OBP stood for Sector Of Intelligence And Security, which we have to obviously update the translation in the English --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence and security, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who within that sector on the night of 13 of July was higher ranking than you and was present at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, no. I think ... I don't remember. I think that General Tolimir wasn't there on the 13th of July. There was General Miletic, and who was there from the security administration? I don't know. I didn't go into their offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said at transcript page 13069 that during the days that you were there you didn't see General Tolimir because he was in the area of Rogatica and Zepa --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just so that we are clear, Zepa was covered by the Rogatica Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So the night of 13 July, which is the day that you arrived at the Main Staff command post from Bijeljina, I think you said, to your knowledge, you were the highest-ranking member of the intelligence and security sector when this particular document was sent. So we see a "sent" time there of 0030 hours, 14 July 1995. That night of 13 July, you were the highest-ranking member of the intelligence and security sector at the Main Staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If Beara was engaged and was away, then it turns out, yes, I was the highest ranking as a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, Radoslav Jankovic was a member of your staff; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the normal chain of events, he would be responsible to report to you; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to go to a different area, if I could. Yesterday I asked you a series of questions about what you knew about the Srebrenica executions and when you knew it. And in several of your answers to both questions put by me and questions put by the Chamber, you indicated that everybody knew about those executions. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I believed that all those who were supposed to know did know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what you said. What you said is on the transcript of the record. And if you say, I want to change what I said, you're free to do so. But that's not what you said yesterday. Let that be clear. And if there's any doubt to that, the parties know how to verify that on the basis of the audio record. And the only question at this moment that was asked was whether you remember that you said what Mr. Vanderpuye put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do remember. If I said "everybody," I misspoke. I couldn't possibly have known that each and every person in the army was aware of it. They didn't hold an assembly to share the information. I said that all those who had that sort of competence must have known, because the operation was carried out in the AOR of the unit and the prisoners were taken through that zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, if you want to change what you said yesterday, please indicate that. But don't tell us now that you said yesterday what the transcript says you didn't say. What you said yesterday: Everyone knew in town, let alone in the army. That's what -- the words you used yesterday. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You -- you said just now the prisoners were taken through the zone. And so yesterday you said that it involved transporting, logistics, engineering. These are all things you said yesterday that required a certain degree of co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think your answer is not recorded in the record.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the movement of prisons is something that everything knew about at the time that they were moved, right, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not everyone could know. I don't know what you mean. If you meant the civilian population and all that, that's absurd. And I would really appreciate it if what I said yesterday, my words yesterday, could be reiterated here to me in my language. It's impossible that I've just said it in those terms, and if I did it was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me read it back to you then. You were asked this question at page -- transcript page 13102 lines 2 to 11, the following question and the following answer: "Q. Let me come right to it then. You knew at the time that you received this information that everyone in the Main Staff knew, including General Mladic, about those crimes, right?" And your answer is: "I can't say that everybody knew. I can't say that. Most did. For example, some of my desk officers may have well been unaware. They were busy with their own thing and did not have much contact with the others but realistically speaking, yes, probably many people knew because it was a sizeable operation. Those people needed to be transported, logistic units engaged, transport organised, engineering -- the engineering corps activated, so many people were probably engaged in it." That's one answer to one question. You were asked another question by the Presiding Judge, which is at transcript page --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- 13101, lines 1 through 15, in a follow-up to a question that I put to you: "Q. Did you not report this crime because you knew that other members of the Main Staff were fully aware of it, both how horrifying it was and of its scale and who committed it?" The Presiding Judge then asked you: "Or was it that the other part of the question or was it that you had no obligation to report?" And your answer is: "Yes, it is it correct. I heard there, as well as from my operative that I talked to, everyone knew. I think even the whole town knew about it, let alone the army." That's just part of what you said yesterday. You stand by that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you could just repeat this segment. Can you reproduce it in Serbian, just that segment where it says the whole town knew let alone the army. If I can hear it again in Serbian. Because in December I said in Bijeljina that I received that information from my operatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be verified, Mr. Salapura, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question to you today is you made a previous reference just now to the prisoners moving through the zone as one of the reasons why people knew or had to know about the crimes. Is that a fair assessment of what you just said?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they were transported. And if that was being done during the day, people probably could see that, the way they were moved, and some people certainly did, but I can't really say everyone. But some did probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who would have to know about something like that, to move prisoners through corps or even through brigades within a corps, whether it's at night, during the day-time, or even if it's moving them from a football stadium to a town nearby? Who would have to know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which nearby town you mean, but whoever ordered the transport to be carried out and the movement of the prisoners, the person who was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: What about the people that would be required to secure the prisoners, would they have to know if the prisoners were moved? Military police, security officers, would they have to know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. Probably those who secured them, who guarded them, yes, they could see that these people were being put on trucks and taken away, or on buses or whatever the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about the people responsible for arranging their exchange during a time of war, would they have to know where the prisoners were or being -- where they were being moved at any given point in time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't say about that. I don't know whether and when they were informed, if they were. There were exchange commissions with the Main Staff and there were also corps commissions for the exchanges of prisoners. Now when it was that they were informed, and they probably were, I really don't know. But I've already told you that I did not have any role. I didn't -- I wasn't involved in that operation at all, so I don't know how it was organised. All I was saying was of a general nature. I can't tell you specifically, you know, so-and-so or so-and-so did that, because I wasn't engaged in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to know is why you say you don't know. Why is it that you say you don't know when, as the chief of intelligence of the intelligence administration of the Main Staff of the VRS, one of your core functions is to extract or obtain intelligence from sources, such as prisoners of war? Why is it that say that you don't know what happened to the prisoners that you saw at the football when one of your core functions is to interrogate them or see that information that is relevant and important for the command and control of the Main Staff and of the army is extracted for the benefit of its commander? Why is that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't our core function. Our core function was to gather all information on the enemy. There was the -- because the Srebrenica operation had already been completed, militarily, and we were the -- the -- the brunt of our operation now was -- the focus of our intelligence activity was on the Tuzla Corps and to see whether they would be moving towards us. Now as for that these zones and units, I don't know exactly and precisely which unit was where. I didn't take part directly in this. There could have been officers at the lower-level battalion perhaps that -- who would want to obtain some information that was relevant to them. Maybe they would have been there, but as far as Srebrenica was concerned, because that had already been completed, that operation, there was nothing of intelligence relevance to us anymore. So our focus moved to the Tuzla Corps. But there could have been officers, security officers, or my officers who would still be involved trying to gather some information because there may have been perhaps within those groups of prisoners those who had committed some crimes during the war and so on. So that would be the type of information that they would want to gather perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask for clarifications. Mr. Salapura, you're saying that -- you say that there could have been some security officers or your officers. And if your officers were there, they would have to make their report that would finally get to you, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would be the battalion officer. I was the chief of the intelligence administration of the Main Staff. So if they thought that there was something relevant, they will send a telegram. I was not involved. I didn't get involved in the work. Do you understand? I was waiting for any day then I was supposed to go back. And I told Maric --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or Mandic that they should go on and work as if I hadn't been there. I was stopped because the traffic was stopped. There was no movement towards Zvornik. So I did not get involved in the work in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, can I stop you, please. My question was very simple. Your subordinates who might have been there would have to report and through the chain of command the report would come to you. Is it so or is it not so? Yes or no. Don't explain anything to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it was assessed that it was relevant, it would arrive. The security officers at the battalion would then inform the brigade officer, and he would, in turn, inform the corps officer. And they would send the information up to me, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I please stop you. May I please stop you. Please, if you can say either yes or no to my question, I'll be happy. Don't give me a story. They would have to report through the chain of command, and the report would get to you; is that the correct procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What -- what would arrive? That there were prisoners there. Yes, there would be information that there were prisoners in this place and in that place and in that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Let me stop you. The record will show that you don't want to answer my question. My question just wanted a yes or no. Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I want to show the witness, if I could, 65 ter 4643.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You'll recognise this, sir, as a document you referred to yesterday or the day before. This is the intelligence support manual that I referred you to in your direct examination. And what I'd like to do first is to go to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- paragraph number 17, which is on page 19 in the English, page 25 in the B/C/S, please. What this refers to are the basic duties of the intelligence organ. In says in commands and staffs of the JNA and TO. And you can see there that it says: "To organise, direct, and co-ordinate overall intelligence and reconnaissance activities," and so forth?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The second thing in this section is: "To constantly gather and process intelligence about the enemy." Right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to take you now to paragraph 198, that's page 59 in the English and page 74 in the B/C/S. And what you can see there is a reference to the process of questioning prisoners of war and defectors. Page 74 in the B/C/S; page 59 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What we can see here is under paragraph 198: "Intelligence organs in commands and staff question prisoners of war and defectors for the purpose of gathering intelligence, through organs of certain specialty that are set up especially for that purpose." Right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so to the extent that prisoners of war are moved from place to place or from one place to another, the intelligence organ has a role in questioning them and gaining information from them. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And prisoners of war are questioned for a variety of purposes; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not dispute that. Yes, they may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So the number of prisoners that you've referred or the prisoners -- the fact that they are moving through a zone of responsibility, either from brigade to brigade or corps to corps, is something that the intelligence sector should be aware of; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the intelligence organ in the battalion would know about that but not intelligence sector. Because this is still within the AOR of the corps. So, yes, the corps organs, they should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The corps organs report to the Main Staff, don't they?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do report the Main Staff, but they would do that in the regular combat report, in the regular intelligence report. There is no rush because Srebrenica had already been taken over. It was a completed operation. So in intelligence interpreters, Srebrenica was not relevant anymore, it was not of interest. The focus of the intelligence operation - and I'm trying to explain this so you can understand - of all the organs within the Drina Corps were now -- the focus was shifted to Tuzla, the Tuzla Corps. We were expecting a counter-attack and in fact it did happen later on an, and there were certain movements and manoeuvres that we monitored. But as for the questioning of these prisoners, there was time for that and it was considered that they would end up in a camp and then the questioning could go on for the next month or so. So there was nothing urgent that could be obtained from them any more. There was no information of such priority that they could provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, you are aware, are you not, that one pressing priority that the VRS had on 13th July when you went down to the Main Staff was a column of thousands of individuals coming up behind the defence lines towards the Zvornik area; right? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were moving towards Tuzla. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thousands of them, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw such persons in Srebrenica even. Yes. And this column, it was moving towards Tuzla, one of them, even towards Srebrenica -- rather, towards Tuzla. I was intercepted on the road. I was stooped because of the operations and that -- that was moving towards Tuzla. I was stopped when I started out. I was stopped at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You issued an order or direction on the 15th of July to jam their communications, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you were aware, at the very least, that there was a large group, some of whom are armed, moving towards the defence lines from the rear from Srebrenica in the direction of Zvornik. You wouldn't consider that pressing information or intelligence information to gain for the benefit of the commander of the Main Staff? You don't think it would have been useful to ask somebody at Nova Kasaba or Sandici about where the column is, how big it is, how may people are there, how armed are they or not, what direction they're going, what communications they have with the 2nd Corps on the other side? You don't think that that would have been useful information to provide to the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that this was information that was collected by the officers at the lower levels, battalions and brigades. And they would then forward to the forward command post, to the commander. And we jammed ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I see that it's time for a break. Could you inform the Chamber how much more time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have just -- well, I have just a couple of questions on this issue, and then I have one document I wanted to show the witness and that should wrap it up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So I would say between 15 minutes and a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to finish in 20 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the break. We'll take a break. But the witness first may leave the courtroom and can follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I ask the attention for the following. An e-mail has been sent to all the parties and to Chamber's staff on the -- I think it was on the 20th of -- or even the 19th of June, about the use of charts with witnesses RM0279, RM316, RM506, and RM507, charts related to intercepts. We have not heard from the Defence whether there are any objections against this way of proceeding. It is not uncommon to use charts, and the Chamber, of course, needs assistance in understanding intercepts. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you already know, Your Honour, we do not like charts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It dumps too many documents on us, so we have to deal in a limited time-frame with more documents that we are used -- supposed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we are never in favour of having those charts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is -- you don't like it, but there's no solid objection against it on legal grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- you referred to the burden it puts upon the Defence, and if that causes major problems. And I think the first few are with a limited number of intercepts. But I would have to look exactly -- the large number is with RM507 and he is scheduled after the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I'm sorry to maybe interrupt you, but we do object not only because it puts a burden on us and we also have to be cautious because we work on a day-by-day basis. So we are not familiar still whether we really have substantial objections to those intercepts or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will have to wait until the witnesses are here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which then means --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- or a few days before when we are ready to cross-examine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the Chamber then only has to consider whether we allow the Prosecution, at this moment, to proceed as suggested and we'll then hear of any further objections at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is allowed to proceed as suggested, and I think it is clear now on the record what the position of the Defence is. Mr. Salapura, this was not very relevant for you, but we started with a small procedural matter. Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Vanderpuye to conclude his re-examination, I would like you to listen to, as you asked, to your own words, spoken yesterday in B/C/S. And the Chamber would very much appreciate if we could again receive interpretation for those words. And if you would just give me a second so that I can have on my one screen my yesterday transcript, and then I'll look at today's transcript on the basis of the audio recording. One second, please. One second. We will play two minutes of your testimony of yesterday so that you are able to see whether it's ill-interpreted or whether it's ill transcribed, as you claimed it may have been. Madam Registrar, could we start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop for a second. Is it possible that we again receive interpretation of those words spoken yesterday so that I am better able to see where there may be a possible problem? There may be no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is possible. The portion that we've just heard was the interpretation from English into B/C/S. The original was English, so we did not interpret it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I do understand, and if you would then -- if we would receive interpretation, especially of the words spoken in B/C/S, because that's what we're focussed on. Then ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters also interpret the B/C/S booth, because that's what we are hearing now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if I would know exactly -- well, of course, then we also know what the witness heard when the question was put to him, so then we have the complete picture. And if you're able to do that, I would be very, very pleased.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we re-start the two minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "So you couldn't even imagine the scale of that. You, as a high-ranking officer of the VRS, did you feel that it was not your responsibility to submit a report, or was it that you did not submit a report because you knew that everybody already knew of these events? Now, did you not report on this crime because you knew that other members of the Main Staff were fully aware of it and the atrocity and the scale of the crime. Now did you - "JUDGE ORIE: Did you -- was this the answer to your other part of your -- of the question or was it the first part of the question? "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Well, I heard from the operatives and everybody already knew about it I think. I think it had already even leaked out into the town, so I believe that it was ongoing. It was in a process. "JUDGE ORIE: Let me then try to see whether I understood your answer correctly. Are you trying to say that you were duty-bound to report on it but it was not necessary to do so because everybody was already -- everybody was already apprised of it; is that how you should under your answer? "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Well, what I learned after I talked to my operatives, that's the gist. "JUDGE ORIE: No, no, you've already replied. Mr. Vanderpuye, you may pose your next question. "MR. VANDERPUYE: Well, I will ask for a clarification. "Q. Colonel, when you say 'everybody knew,' do you mean everyone at the Main Staff, is that it? "A. Well, the then-organs ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this having been played. Do you have any comment on having now listened to the B/C/S version of what you testified yesterday? You earlier said you may have misspoke. You may have misspoken. Is there anything you would like to add at this moment because you asked for the verification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is all right. It is correct. I said all of that. Everybody knew when my subordinates informed me and when you ask whether the command organs knew, I said everybody knew. And I meant that part, the inner circle, as it were. And I said it had already leaked in the town that part of the -- some of the people, of the civilian population, they also knew. I didn't mean that everyone in the town knew. So it's all right. So when I said "everyone," or "all," I meant the staff, those who dealt with those issues and worked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noted there are some slight differences between the translation of today and the translation of yesterday. The Chamber will have it verified especially where the words are used, either "it leaked into town," or whether "everyone knew in town," that may need some further attention. We'll ask for a verification, especially of that portion. Then, Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, at the break I'd asked you some questions about who would have known about these crimes at the time that they were being committed. And I asked you about whether or not the military police would know, whether or not the police would know, and whether or not those who were interrogating or responsible for interrogating prisoners would know, and exchange commissions, and so on. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it correct that those units or people would know at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two things here. The Tribunal is focussed on Srebrenica, and that is the main problem. For my service and for me, this is a tactical problem, whereas I dealt with strategic problems and the focus of my work was in the west and the service overall. At the moment when Srebrenica was taken over, it became irrelevant to us. The focus of the intelligence work was shifted. And I repeat that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura -- Mr. Salapura -- Mr. Salapura, why not answer the question? The question simply was whether it's correct that those units or people would know at the time. Would they know, or would they not know at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, those units that were -- that dealt with it, they probably knew. They had to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The units that dealt with it had to report what they were doing to the superior organs; right? That's how a military works, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Not "probably." My question is: Do you know that to be true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it ought to be, but it is up to the competent commanding or senior officer who will decide when the reporting will take place. I can tell you that for the duration of my stay at Han Pijesak, I did not get that involved into work by Mamlic told me that he was not receiving information from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, when I give you a sign that I want to intervene, you should stop speaking. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please abide by that. What happens here is the following. Mr. Vanderpuye, you're asking a question whether these units had to report what they were doing to the superior organs. That is a question dealing with what the duties were. Now, the witness apparently is focussed on what happened, whether or not in line with the duties, that creates this confusion. Because if the witness says "probably," then he wants to say - at least that's how I understand him - that that is the way it should be and probably happened but he doesn't know. Now, this is the result of asking not questions of fact but, rather, questions asking about what should have been done instead of what was done. That creates the confusion, and that is the reason why factual questions to a witness of fact avoid such confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I show you, please, P1589. Colonel, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, and I recall it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's -- it's from you and it's signed by you, is it -- is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this is the document that referred to the jamming of communications of - as it reads here - part of the -- scattered parts of the 26th Division. It should say "28th Division," as we can see in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we will submit a request to amend this translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But you can see on the left of your -- of the document in the B/C/S, and we can blow that up so that everyone can see what division it refers to specifically, it's in the second line.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th Division. The document states the "28th" and the translation the "26th."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And specifically this is the direction or order, as it were, to start jamming radio communications between the 28th Division and the 2nd Corps of the ABiH, yes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that refers to the situation that was unfolding with the movement of the 28th Division or parts of the 28th Division through the territory to the rear of the Zvornik Brigade towards Baljkovica; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And on the other side of the Zvornik Brigade, that is, on the other side of the defence line is where the 2nd Corps was situated at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You issued this order based on information that was relayed to you, I take it, at the Main Staff during the period of time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most probably. I can't be fully certain. We probably intercepted information from the 2nd Corps that they would be mounting an attack in order to join up with these scattered groups, and we got that through electronic reconnaissance, I suppose. I issued a task to start jamming the radio communications of the 2nd Corps units. The units that were mounting an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to clarify that that's the order that you issued and that it was based upon information that reached you at the Main Staff of the VRS. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One point. The word used was "order" and the document before us is not an order. The witness did say repeatedly that he was not in a position to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether order or not, the Chamber will focus on the text of the document. And whether the words "start doing something" is an order or a suggestion or a advice or a -- we'll consider that. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to just take you to the next day, the 14th of July -- rather, the previous day, 14th of July, 1995. And you remember that this is the day that you are recorded in the duty officer's notebook of the Zvornik Brigade passing on a message to get in contact for Beara, Colonel Beara, and Drago Nikolic to get in contact with your subordinate, Major Pavle Golic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 8227 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to show you a document. You were asked about your duties and essentially what you were doing between the time that you arrived at Crna Rijeka on the 13th and the time that you left, about the 18th of July, 1995. This is a --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is the diary of an individual named Bob Djurdjevic. You can see his name at the bottom. And in this diary, he records a meeting that he had with you on the 14th of July, 1995. First, do you recognise the name, Bob Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show -- I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do remember Djurdjevic, Bob. Yes, I think I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have been informed that we actually do have a fully translated version of this -- no? A partial translated version of this under 65 ter 25979. So if we could call that one up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do is to take you first to page 44. I don't think we have a translation of that but just so that we can see the date that we're talking, and then we'll move up to the section I want to discuss with you. Here you can see it reflects the date of 14 July 1995. And if we can just page in sequence up to page 47, we'll see the reference that I want to discuss with you. And also we can see that there's no intervening date. This is the reference that we have concerning Mr. Djurdjevic's meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my name is mentioned mere.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we do have the B/C/S translation of this. So if we could show this to the witness, I'd like him to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'd like to see it. I don't know what this is about. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we've got it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the English has disappeared in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it refers to a meeting that he had with you, 14 July 1995. It says: "Lunch at the officers' mess plus a meeting at officer Djukic's office in Han Pijesak with Colonel Salapura," PS, as he designates you in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, could you guide us to where the date exactly appears?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The date was at page 44 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. So that you say it's the previous day -- the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't think it is the previous page. This is it page 47. But we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes 44 -- no, it's fine. I'll find it, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this document, Colonel, you can see Mr. Djurdjevic recalls a meeting he had with you on the afternoon between 1345 and 1545 hours on 14 July 1995. Have you had a chance to look a little bit at the first entry there, under "lunch"? He talks about a --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does it refresh your recollection about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Believe me, I don't remember. It was probably a short meeting, perhaps even an accidental meeting. And it could have been at Han Pijesak where the rear was, the logistics. I see that mention is made of the officers' mess.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. He mentions that you also suggested that you go upstairs where you can talk in peace and that you ended up in the same office which belonged to General Djukic. That's in the second paragraph of -- I'm sorry, in the third paragraph under "lunch" --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I'm not denying it. I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. What I want to ask you about we can find on the next page, in particular. I think we go to the same -- the next page in both languages. And you'll see at the top, Mr. Djurdjevic has written down the following. It says: "War to extinction." And then he quotes you as follows: "This war will not be over when some politicians sign a peace treaty. This war will end when one of the three nations in Bosnia becomes extinct. We have to make sure we're not the one." Do you remember saying that to Mr. Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I don't remember ever holding such views or positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Djurdjevic testified in the Karadzic case in 2012?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the 7th of March, 2012, he testified in that case and he was asked this question and gave this answer. Reading the same paragraph, or rather, the same quote to him, he was asked this question: "Does that accurately reflect what Colonel Salapura told you," and this is, by the way, for the benefit of the Chamber, transcript of those proceedings page 25917, 7 March 2012. "Does this accurately reflect what Colonel Salapura told you?" And his answer was: "It does." Do you deny making it or is it that you can't recall saying it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I don't remember this detail. And I think that I've stated it already for perhaps 20 times that the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina would not be permanently resolved for as long as two peoples would be joining up against the third people. And I stand by this today. And as for this, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, I instructed you when I made clear to you that I want to intervene that you should stop speaking. Is that clear to you? Once again. Otherwise, I will take over the examination in the way I want it to be conducted. The question was not about what you may have said, at what point in time, about similar things. The question was about whether you remember or you do not remember that meeting and whether, if you remember, that this is what you said, or that this is not what you said; or that you just don't remember whether you said such a thing. The start of the answer was related to the question, where you said, I don't remember this detail. Which I understand to be that - and I'll ask you that - that you don't remember that you would have spoken those words. At the same time, it suggests that you do remember that you had a conversation with this person. So, therefore, two questions: Do you remember to have had a conversation with person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second: You do not remember to have used those words, or do you have a recollection that you certainly did not use those words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember ever using such words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also not during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I don't remember using them, and I believe I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye. And next time, Mr. Salapura, if, again, you think that to continue talking when I intervene that that is the appropriate way of conduct in this courtroom, we'll take a different course. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That just about does it for me and I'd like to tender this -- this document. I suppose I will tender just the part that I've -- that I've used with Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Not. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you referred to two 65 ter numbers. Now which one -- is it the second one --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's 25 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that is the one you wish to tender and we have it translated. Has it been uploaded already? It has not been uploaded already. Therefore we reserve a number for it, pending the uploading of this document. Madam Registrar, the number would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would ask for a suffix perhaps for the 65 ter number 25979A, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 275 -- I think it's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will receive number P1590, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. It is a number reserved and the Chamber would like to be informed as soon as it is uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The document ID ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm informed that I should request to replace the translation of D00306, that was the document referred to the intelligence and security service, which erroneously previously referred to it as just the intelligence sector. There was a 13 July document, document ID 00663716-ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there were two potential translation problems identified. The first one was the one you mentioned. The other one was the two or not, who was the addressee of that document. Has that been verified as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand they've both been addressed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They've both been addressed. Then hereby leave is granted to replace the English translation in e-court, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we look at the English translation of D306 at this moment, which is now uploaded Madam Registrar, so that we can see what has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that the Defence will also carefully look at the new English translation and see whether there's any problem remaining. For the time being now, then, we will -- the document can now be admitted into evidence. There was no objection. It was even ... Mr. Mladic has an audio problem apparently. Could the usher assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we have any objections to this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think even that -- that you tendered the document, Mr. Stojanovic, so that there's no objection goes without saying, I would say. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. But, of course, it's impossible for me to see what the differences are between the initial translation and this one in this one moment. That's why I expressed this reservation, because I can't see the differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's any problem, you may revisit the matter. Madam Registrar, it was -- D306 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I am not certain whether I should instruct you also to remove it as an MFI, but I think it's implicit in admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we give an opportunity to the Defence for further examination of the witness, the Chamber would have a few questions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, could you explain to me again what exactly was the reason that you travelled to the area and were trying to find out where Mr. Mladic was? What exactly was it that you wanted to see him about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point was to inform General Mladic that the Croatian army was preparing an attack on the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, that the Krajina would not be able to hold out for long because of the internal problems that it had, and that the activities would spill over to the territory of the western part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that the only reason why you wanted to see him and what you wanted to talk about with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some other issues that I had, but I don't think I even had time to relay them because General Mladic was in a hurry, we had to interrupt our conversation, and I left. I had another meeting there with some -- or rather, I had some -- a meeting with some diplomatic represents in Belgrade, like, for instance, the Japanese representative who recommended that we accord a fair treatment to the prisoners of war and that we draw as much publicity to it as we can --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And can the witness repeat the last thing he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last thing you said, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since our image in the world was already a negative one, and I'm referring to the coverage in the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, that other meeting with some diplomatic persons in Belgrade, had that taken place? And what -- was that a matter you wanted to discuss with Mr. Mladic or did it still have to take place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That meeting was already held at the time when I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said there was a third subject you would like to discuss with Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I don't remember anymore what it was. I have to think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as soon as you remember --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was the main issues. Anything else could only have been of secondary importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said: "... we had to interrupt our conversation and I left." Now, what did you discuss with Mr. Mladic before the conversation was interrupted? Was it the Krajina matter or was it the issue you're -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed the Krajina issue. I relayed what the problem was, and then I also shared a number of details as to why I believed the defence would be short-lived and what sort of consequences this might have for us, et cetera. I think that General Mladic had another meeting that he go to -- he had to go to or something else. At any rate, we just shook hands. I went my way and he went his, with his escort. I think he had another meeting or perhaps an interview he had to go to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the issue of the prisoners of war, you did not, as you had heard from -- by a Japanese diplomate. That was never the subject of any discussion at that point in time with Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your previous testimony, you told us that the -- there was a kind of an offer for assistance to resolve any potential problems in relation to prisoners of war. Did you -- and I could read that to you. "We could perhaps help out in changing this image of you that the world has," that apparently were the words spoken or the message given to you by the Japanese diplomat. Did you consider that not of greatest priority at that moment to discuss --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you didn't find time to do that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said briefly what it was I was supposed to discuss with the General. He waved his hand by way of hello and he went on his way, so what were you to do? We were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably had more pressing business rather than just continue this conversation with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we also saw you in a rather relaxed atmosphere in the house of a person where it did not give the impression that everyone was in such a hurry, that not even two or three lines could be spent on what you considered a very important matter. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to. I know that he went there. I can't recall now whether that was something that had been scheduled earlier or something, I really don't know. But that you saw me while I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You could have stopped after "I don't know what you are referring to," because I would have explained to you that I was referring to a video image where you are at -- just behind a lady. I think it was shown to you during examination and you identified yourself as being there in a -- could I say in a family environment, where Mr. Mladic had a conversation with that lady about her job and whether she would work again in a similar job. That is what I'm referring to. That -- that didn't give me the impression that such matters of huge importance could in no way have been discussed with Mr. Mladic. Do you have an explanation as how you spent time on these matters and not find time for discussion of very urgent and important matters?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what less important matters we were discussing. I didn't talk about anything in that house. This was before the meeting with General Mladic. I wanted to talk with him, but he sort of just gestured and then led me with him towards that house. So he was the one who spoke to this woman, not me. I just listened on to the conversation. I can't recall what it was about. I think this was shown on TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I leave that explanation for the time being. Not having had an opportunity to bring this in a conversation to the attention of Mr. Mladic, what did you do afterwards to bring this very important matter to his intention -- to his attention? If you did anything; if not, please tell us. If you did, please tell us what you did.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nothing. And on my way back, I saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's an answer. Did you bring it to anyone else's attention, this urgent problem raised by the Japanese diplomat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue was not urgent; but, no, I did not inform anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. I have another question. You have seen a number of documents, you've commented on some of them, documents which suggest that you were not just waiting in order to be able to leave and get the medical care you needed but that you played a role in the events. Do you remember others talking about your role, issuing whether or not an order but at least telling who should jam the communications of the other party? The -- you've seen a number of these reports. Is there any fact you could tell us about which explains why others, and including yourself in that instruction, to jam the communications? Put you in a position of at least some involvement in the events, whereas you're telling us again and again that you played no role whatsoever. Do you have any fact which we should know in order to better understand the discrepancy between your version and the version which is depicted in some of these documents that have been put to you and which we looked at?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that when I came to my room at the command post, I only found Major Mamlic there and the staff-sergeant. It is possible that Mamlic was there when these people came or maybe he had been out to lunch or had gone to see Miletic, General Miletic.
